recipes.name: Build hashed math from f64 + - * / and sqrt: the same bits on IEEE CPUs, wasm engines and in const eval
recipes.what: The IEEE 754 basic operations (+, -, *, /, sqrt) are correctly rounded (round to nearest, ties to even) in Rust and in WebAssembly, neither flushes subnormals, and rustc's const evaluator computes them in a host-independent soft-float, so a computation built only from them has one bit pattern natively, in every wasm engine and at compile time; only NaN bit patterns may differ.
recipes.how: Keep hashed arithmetic in f64 built from `+ - * /` and `f64::sqrt` (plus bit operations such as `abs`, comparisons and exact int-to-float conversions). Prove agreement the way the checks do: run one chain natively and in wasm and compare `to_bits()`. A 100 000-step chain that also makes a subnormal every step digests to 7853152472807335572 on x86-64 at -O0 and at -O and in wasm32 under node 22's V8; `50.0 * PI / 180.0` is 0x3febecde5da115a9 as a const, at run time natively, and at run time in wasm (4606035483714196905). Derived constants may be `const`/`const fn` (float ops in const fn since 1.82; `mul_add` const since 1.94), but a transcendental in a const is E0015. Leave the floating-point environment alone: Rust assumes the default rounding with denormals-are-zero off, and changing MXCSR's rounding or DAZ bits is immediate UB (`_mm_setcsr` docs); wasm operators round to nearest, ties to even, unless an operator says otherwise (trunc, floor, ...), in non-stop mode, and there is no mode to change.
recipes.rust_version: any stable (semantics per RFC 3514); float ops in const fn 1.82+; mul_add const 1.94+; checked on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: RFC 3514's own caveat: 32-bit x86 returns floats in x87 registers, altering NaN payloads, and i586 targets use x87 even more pervasively; that is a native 32-bit concern, not wasm32. The guarantee is per operation: a different order ((a+b)+c vs a+(b+c)), an f32 intermediate or a transcendental breaks bit equality. NaN bits made at compile time need not match run time (std docs). On the no_std target wasm32v1-none `f64::sqrt` does not exist on stable (E0599; core's float math is unstable), so a no_std law calls `libm::sqrt`.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs states the rule in its header ('No other operation than add, sub, mul, div, and sqrt') for `step` and `resolve_pair`; rapier_law.rs's own arithmetic (`canon_quat`, the collider centres and half-extents in `build_world`) stays inside it apart from min/max on positive half-extents, and CLIMB_ANGLE / SLIDE_ANGLE are const-evaluated basic ops. FLAGS.md's 'Nothing in the flags flushes subnormals, so they stay subnormals' holds on both sides: Rust treats a changed DAZ/FTZ state as UB, and wasm defines no flush mode. This is why V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore can print one golden.

recipes.name: Expect a*b+c to stay unfused: rustc never contracts, mul_add always rounds once, wasm has no scalar fma
recipes.what: rustc never turns `a * b + c` into a fused multiply-add, not at -O and not with `-C target-feature=+fma`; `f64::mul_add` always rounds once, and on wasm32 it is a software fma compiled into the module (no import); wasm 3.0 has no scalar fma instruction, so hardware-chosen fusion can only enter through relaxed SIMD's relaxed_madd; the stable opt-in to contraction since 1.98.0 is the `algebraic_*` family.
recipes.how: Write `a * b + c` when the law means two roundings (what a JS kernel computes). Write `a.mul_add(b, c)` only when you want IEEE fusedMultiplyAdd on every target: the std docs guarantee 'the rounded infinite-precision result', and it differs from the unfused form (inputs 1+eps, 1-eps, -1 give -4.930380657631324e-32 fused and 0 unfused on x86-64 at -O0, at -O with +fma, and in wasm32). Keep `algebraic_add/sub/mul/div/rem` out of the law (the rust-currency lane covers them; a source grep for `algebraic_` refuses them). Keep relaxed SIMD disabled (`-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd`) and let T3's opcode lint prove that no relaxed instruction reached the binary.
recipes.rust_version: any (no contraction); mul_add const 1.94+; algebraic_* stable 1.98.0+
recipes.gotchas: 'Rust may contract a*b+c like a C compiler' is wrong: RFC 3514 precludes it because rounding would change. The reverse mistake is treating `mul_add` as a speed hint that equals `a*b+c`: it is a different result, and without FMA hardware it is a library call. SIMD crates choose per target: wide 1.7.1's `f64x2::mul_add` fuses on x86 with the `fma` feature and on aarch64 NEON and rounds twice elsewhere; relaxed_madd may be fused or unfused, fixed per environment.
recipes.engine_note: FLAGS.md's 'Fused multiply-add is not in that set. It arrives only with relaxed SIMD, which this build disables' is right about hardware fusion, but an explicit `mul_add` in solver/src or in a dependency still yields a fused result (a deterministic software fma), so the sentence is safest as 'no implicit fusion; mul_add only where written'. solver/src at e5fbcb9 has no mul_add; the rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 and parry3d-f64 0.30.2 sources have none either (grep this session). T3's relaxed-SIMD opcode lint is the gate for the only hardware-dependent fusion path.

recipes.name: Keep std sin, cos, exp, ln, powf, atan2 and hypot out of hashed math; call the Cargo.lock-pinned libm
recipes.what: std documents sin, cos, exp, ln, powf, atan2 and hypot as 'Unspecified precision' (varies by platform and Rust version). Natively they are the platform C library's (on this Windows host each of the seven disagrees with the libm crate somewhere in a 100 000-input sweep); on wasm32-unknown-unknown they are compiled into the module from the toolchain's own copy of libm in compiler-builtins, which today matches libm 0.2.16 for sin but not for hypot.
recipes.how: For any transcendental whose bits can reach state or a hash, call one pinned implementation explicitly: the `libm` crate (`libm::sin`, `libm::cos`, `libm::atan2`, `libm::hypot`, `libm::pow`, `libm::exp`, `libm::log`), whose version Cargo.lock pins. Measured: wasm32 `f64::sin` over the sweep digests to 1810793848087136966, exactly libm 0.2.16's digest, and the module imports nothing; wasm32 `f64::hypot` digests to -4090065345391819473 against libm 0.2.16's 727198713234182705, because rustc 1.98.1's in-tree hypot.rs is a CORE-MATH port while libm 0.2.16 ships a different (SPLIT/sq) algorithm.
recipes.gotchas: 'IEEE 754 makes sin portable' is wrong: RFC 3514's guarantees cover the basic operations only, and std gives the transcendentals unspecified precision. On wasm32 the std functions are deterministic across engines (they are wasm code) but move with the toolchain, not with Cargo.lock. Two careful implementations can both be deterministic and still disagree (hypot here); determinism comes from pinning one copy, not from accuracy. On no_std targets there is no stable `f64::sin` at all.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src (lib.rs, rapier_law.rs at e5fbcb9) calls only sqrt, min and max, so the crate's own code is clean; mirror T3 pin 7, which refuses Math.sin/cos/tan/atan2/hypot in JS scene builders, with a Rust source test over solver/src. The dependency graph is not clean: parry and glamx reach the toolchain's log2, acos and cos through inherent calls (see the rust-toolchain.toml recipe).

recipes.name: Know what rapier3d-f64 0.35.3's enhanced-determinism switches: libm, IndexMap, canonical zeros, not SIMD
recipes.what: `enhanced-determinism` = simba's `libm_force` (an optional dependency on the libm crate, so simba's ComplexField/RealField math on f64 calls libm) plus parry's flag (indexmap, glamx/libm, glamx/scalar-math). In code it makes parry's HashMap/HashSet an IndexMap/IndexSet with a pointer-width-independent FxHasher32, drains joint wake-up/join sets in order, canonicalises -0.0 in the warm-start impulses it stores, and refuses `simd8` with compile_error!. It does not switch off parry's 4-lane `wide` types.
recipes.how: Keep the feature on and never add `parallel` or `simd8` beside it. What it buys the wasm law: map iteration fixed by the insert/remove sequence, simba and glam transcendentals pinned by Cargo.lock, no -0.0 in stored impulses. Measured in the oracle, which links the solver's feature set: parry's HashMap iterates [5, 1, 3] in insertion order and has IndexMap's `swap_remove`; `SIMD_WIDTH` is 4 and `SimdReal` is `simba::simd::wide_simd_impl::WideF64x4`; simba's `ComplexField::sin` and glam's `DQuat::from_rotation_y` equal `libm::sin` bit for bit on 100 000 inputs where std's `f64::sin` does not.
recipes.rust_version: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3, parry3d-f64 0.30.2, simba 0.10.2, glam 0.33.10 (via glamx 0.3.1), wide 1.7.1
recipes.gotchas: Correcting a common recollection: the flag does not turn SIMD off. parry 0.30.2 says the wide types 'are always used, whatever the platform' (scalar code on wasm32 without simd128), and `glamx/scalar-math` only affects glam's f32 SIMD types (glam's f64 types never use SIMD). `libm_force` is not in simba's [features] table: it is the implicit feature of an optional dependency renamed from libm. simba's `simd_mul_add` for WideF64x4 is not gated by libm_force and fuses on aarch64 NEON and x86+fma when compiled natively. The flag cannot reroute inherent calls such as `x.log2()` on an f64 (see the rust-toolchain.toml recipe). Without it parry's maps are hashbrown with foldhash's FixedState.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml enables the feature, and FLAGS.md's 'This version has no simd-stable or simd-nightly feature; wide is still a transitive crate' matches parry 0.30.2. The flag matters most for host bindings: a native Godot/Unreal build keeps equal to the wasm law only where libm_force, glamx/libm and canonicalize_zero reach; `WideF64x4::simd_mul_add` would fuse on a native aarch64 build (no call site at these versions, by grep). The IndexMap order depends on the insert/remove sequence, which T2 restore must replay (restore-internals owns the details).

recipes.name: Canonicalize -0.0 to +0.0 before to_bits() feeds a hash: equal values, different bits
recipes.what: `0.0 == -0.0` is true but their bits differ (0x0000000000000000 vs 0x8000000000000000), so a hash over `to_bits()` splits equal states; the sign survives the wasm-to-JS boundary, `total_cmp` orders -0.0 before +0.0, and min/max may return either zero on a tie.
recipes.how: Canonicalize at every point where bits are stored or hashed: `if x == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { x }` (the engine's `canon`) or `x + 0.0` (Rapier's `canonicalize_zero`; -0.0 + 0.0 is +0.0 under round to nearest). Both leave NaN alone, so refuse NaN separately. Shown: raw `mix_f64` of 0.0 and -0.0 differ while the canonical mix is equal; in wasm `canon_zero(-0.0)` returns 0 while an identity export hands -0 to JS.
recipes.gotchas: Canonicalizing only inside the hash still lets -0.0 flow on: 1.0 / -0.0 is -inf, so canonicalize where the value is written too (write_body does). `x + 0.0` looks like dead code to a reviewer or a refactor; name it. `abs()` also clears the sign but changes negative numbers. Sorting by `total_cmp` without canonicalizing separates keys that compare equal.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs canonicalizes in `write_body` (every stored field), `canon_quat`, `push_f64` (the snapshot) and the exported `canon_zero`, and Rapier 0.35.3 canonicalizes the warm-start impulses it writes under enhanced-determinism. One path hashes raw bits: `signature()` feeds collider and height values to `mix_f64`, and `same_sig` compares the result, so a quantum whose record writes -0.0 where the previous one wrote +0.0 reloads the world and drops the warm-start cache (build.mjs's `box.qx || 0` canonicalizes only the quaternion's x, y, z). That is a reading of the code, not an observed failure; canon before mix_f64 closes it.

recipes.name: Refuse NaN or map it to one bit pattern before hashing: its sign and payload are the engine's choice
recipes.what: NaN != NaN, and the bits of a NaN produced by arithmetic are nondeterministic in both Rust and wasm (the sign always; the payload within the options each spec lists), may differ between const eval and run time, and V8 on this x86-64 host returns 0xfff8000000000000 (sign set) for 0/0 while `f64::NAN` is 0x7ff8000000000000; `total_cmp` still gives a total order (-NaN < -inf < ... < -0 < +0 < ... < +inf < +NaN) where `partial_cmp` returns None.
recipes.how: Refuse NaN at every boundary the law reads or writes (the engine's `bad()`), or map any NaN to `f64::from_bits(0x7ff8000000000000)` before `to_bits()` reaches a hash: in wasm the mapped 0/0 is 9221120237041090560 whatever the host picked. Sort with `sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b))`, never `partial_cmp(..).unwrap()` (a NaN makes it panic, exit 101). Do not branch on `is_sign_negative()` of a NaN.
recipes.rust_version: total_cmp 1.62+; NaN rules documented from 1.82; checked on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: `f64::NAN`'s own bits may change across Rust versions and targets (std docs), so even a constant NaN is not a stable hash input. The wasm 3.0 deterministic profile (positive canonical NaNs) is a separate spec profile; the engine measured here returned a sign-set NaN, so write code for the full profile. A different CPU architecture may pick a different sign for the same 0/0, which is exactly what the ARM64 lane would expose if a NaN ever reached a hash.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs refuses NaN in `signature`, `write_body`, `canon_quat` and `integrate`, and lib.rs's `step` returns 0 on a NaN pose, so no body NaN is hashed. `push_contact` hashes warm-start impulses through `push_f64`, whose `canon` passes a NaN through with the engine's bits; adding `bad()` there (or the one-pattern map) makes the refusal cover every hashed field before the T3 ARM64 lane compares goldens.

recipes.name: Write the min/max tie rule yourself: f64::max(-0.0, 0.0) changes with context, minimum/maximum are nightly
recipes.what: f64::min/max ignore a single NaN (IEEE 754-2019 minimumNumber/maximumNumber) but may return either zero on a -0.0/+0.0 tie; f64::minimum/maximum (NaN-propagating, -0 < +0) are still unstable on 1.98.1 (E0658, feature float_minimum_maximum, #91079); wasm's fmin/fmax propagate NaN and order the zeros; JS Math.min/max return NaN for any NaN argument and treat -0 as smaller than +0 (Math.min(0, -0) is -0, Math.max(-0, 0) is 0).
recipes.how: Where the result can reach state or a hash, spell the tie rule out (as lib.rs's js_min/js_max do) or canonicalize the zero after min/max. Shown with rustc 1.98.1: the same expression `n.max(p)` with n = -0.0 and p = +0.0 returns 0.0 in one function and -0.0 in another where `p.max(n)` was computed beside it, natively at -O and in wasm at -O, while native -O0 gives 0.0 in both (a guess at the cause: the optimiser treats max as commutative and reuses the neighbour's result).
recipes.gotchas: `x.max(0.0)` does not reliably turn -0.0 into +0.0, and `(-0.0).clamp(0.0, 1.0)` returns -0.0 (measured); canonicalize explicitly. A result that looks stable in one build can flip after an unrelated edit or a toolchain bump, which a golden hash then reports as a law change. Rust's f64::min is neither wasm's fmin nor JS's Math.min: those two propagate NaN and order the zeros, Rust's ignores a single NaN and may return either zero.
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs's `js_min`/`js_max` (the overlap in `resolve_pair`) implement JS's zero ordering explicitly, so the box step does not depend on the tie rule. Their NaN behaviour is asymmetric and unlike Math.min: js_min(1, NaN) = 1 but js_min(NaN, 1) = NaN, harmless while `step` returns 0 on a NaN pose. rapier_law.rs's `half.x.min(half.z)` and `(half.y - radius).max(0.0)` act on strictly positive half-extents, so no zero tie arises there.

recipes.name: Treat rust-toolchain.toml as part of the law: the solver links the toolchain's own log2, acos, cos and sin
recipes.what: Inherent calls such as `x.log2()` or `x.acos()` on an f64 resolve to std's method (inherent methods are searched before trait methods, and a `#![no_std]` crate that links std sees them), so libm_force cannot reroute them; in parry 0.30.2's bvh_optimize.rs and glamx 0.3.1's eigen3.rs the ComplexField import is compiled only without std. On wasm32 those std methods are compiler-builtins' copy of libm, pinned by the toolchain, not by Cargo.lock.
recipes.how: Treat a toolchain bump like a libm bump: rerun the goldens and behaviour numbers before accepting it. Shown in the oracle: with ComplexField in scope `a.sin()` is std's (rustc even reports the import unused) while `ComplexField::sin` is libm's; a no_std crate with `extern crate std` compiles `root.log2()` as parry's BVH optimizer writes it. Today the toolchain's acos, log2 and cos in wasm equal libm 0.2.16 over 100 000-input sweeps (digests in the checks) while this Windows host's C runtime does not; hypot shows the two copies can part. A cheap gate: list `compiler_builtins::math::libm_math::*` names from the wasm name section (present in the scratch release build measured here) of every built solver and diff the list on bumps.
recipes.gotchas: Grepping a dependency for `libm::` or trusting 'enhanced-determinism = libm everywhere' misses inherent calls; only the built binary tells you which math is linked. The same calls compiled natively (host bindings) use the platform C library, so a native law would diverge where the wasm law does not. Equality with libm today is a measurement, not a contract.
recipes.engine_note: Measured on a scratch copy of solver/ at e5fbcb9 (cargo +1.98.1 build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --locked): si_solver.wasm's name section lists libm::math::{sin, cos, sqrt, acos, asin, atan, atan2, sincos, floor, ceil, copysign} and compiler_builtins::math::libm_math::{sin, cos, acos, log2}. A wasmparser call graph reaches log2 from `solver_load`/`solver_step` through `BroadPhaseBvh::update` and parry's `Bvh::optimize_incremental`, whose `.log2()` feeds a `.round()` that sets how many subtrees to rebuild; acos/cos are reached from `MassProperties + MassProperties` through glamx `symmetric_eigen`; sin/cos also through the joint builders, which the law does not use. Whether any of these moves the golden is unmeasured; the toolchain pin (1.98.1) is what holds them.

recipes.name: Hash only IndexMap, BTreeMap or sorted order: a fixed hasher does not fix HashMap order across targets
recipes.what: std's HashMap is randomly seeded (SipHash 1-3 today) and iterates in arbitrary order; hashbrown 0.17.1's default is foldhash's randomly initialised RandomState; a fixed hasher fixes the seed, not the iteration order across targets: the same 1000 inserts into a std HashMap with a fixed FNV hasher iterate differently on x86-64 and in wasm32, while a BTreeMap iterates identically (and foldhash does not even promise equal hash values across platforms).
recipes.how: For anything that can reach a hash or a snapshot use `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` (key order), `IndexMap` (insert/remove order, independent of the hasher; give it a fixed hasher such as `Xxh3Builder::new()` if you want reproducible hash values too), or a Vec sorted by a stable id. With IndexMap prefer `shift_remove` (keeps relative order) when order is part of the record; `swap_remove` moves the last entry into the hole but is still deterministic given the same operation sequence. Keep std HashMap/HashSet for lookups only. Measured: HashMap(fixed FNV) order digest 7883764408781778729 on x86-64 vs 415840167048917935 in wasm32; BTreeMap 4523094667136758445 on both.
recipes.rust_version: any; std::hash::RandomState path 1.76+; hashbrown 0.17.1; foldhash 0.2.0; indexmap 2.14.2
recipes.gotchas: 'Use FxHash/foldhash with a fixed seed and the map is deterministic' holds only for one target and one library version: foldhash itself warns against expecting consistent output across versions or platforms, and std documents HashMap order as arbitrary. hashbrown's `DefaultHashBuilder` is randomly initialised. rustc-hash's FxHasher depends on the pointer size; parry wrote FxHasher32 so that it does not.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src holds no hash map; bodies and colliders are index-ordered static arrays and the snapshot sorts contact pairs by collider handle before hashing (rebuild_snapshot). Rapier's own maps are IndexMap<FxHasher32> under enhanced-determinism. Any map added for mesh collision or host bindings should be a BTreeMap or IndexMap on the hashed path.

recipes.name: Gate toolchain and Cargo.lock bumps on goldens plus a libm canary; keep fixed-point for integer-exact parts
recipes.what: Results move on a bump through three mechanisms, each measured here: a libm version changes an algorithm (rustc 1.98.1's in-tree hypot returns 0x4018842a6ab3fa86 where libm 0.2.16 returns ...85 for the same input), a dependency reorders a sum (floating-point addition is not associative), and codegen changes tie choices such as min/max of zeros. Fixed-point arithmetic removes the float-specific classes (reassociation, NaN, signed zero, platform libm) but not the need for a gate.
recipes.how: Keep both pins (rust-toolchain.toml and Cargo.lock) and move them only through a gate: the golden hash, the behaviour numbers and the T4 course, plus a Rust canary test that asserts the bits of the few libm outputs the law depends on, so a lockfile bump fails by name before a golden moves. Shown: `(0.1+0.2)+0.3` is 0x3fe3333333333334 and `0.1+(0.2+0.3)` is ...33; the harmonic sum to 1000 differs forwards and backwards; the same values as Q32.32 integers (what `fixed`'s I32F32 stores) sum identically both ways. Use `fixed` (1.31.0) for new integer-exact subsystems, not for the physics law: Rapier and parry are f64 code.
recipes.gotchas: A digest-only gate says that something moved, not what; the canary and the behaviour numbers name it. A bump stays silent until a scene reaches the changed path, so the golden scenes must exercise what the law uses (the BVH optimizer's log2 matters only when its rounding decision flips). Fixed-point is not free: range is limited, overflow is an error class of its own (the crate offers Wrapping, Saturating and Strict wrappers), and the law would have to leave Rapier.
recipes.engine_note: Mirrors T4 pin 6, which makes any bump of the toolchain or of rapier3d-f64 rerun the course before a golden may move; extend the same rule to libm, simba and glam(x) in Cargo.lock, add the canary as a `cargo test` in solver/, and list toolchain-supplied libm symbols from the built wasm (see the rust-toolchain.toml recipe) so the review sees which pin a change came through.
